learn.hook: What if the whole planet stopped, just for a few seconds, at the same time? A Nobel-winning poet asks us to try.
points: Poet: Pablo Neruda, a Chilean poet and diplomat who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971.
'Keeping Quiet' was written in Spanish and translated into English by Alastair Reid; it is in free verse.
Opening: the poet asks us to count to twelve and keep still, all over the earth, for once.
In that moment no one would speak in any language, and we would not move our arms.

example.q: Why does the poet want no one to speak 'in any language'?
steps: Languages can divide people into groups.
Silence is shared by everyone in the same way.
So a common silence unites all humanity.
example.answer: Because silence is universal; without language barriers, all people would share one moment together.

learn.reallife: India observes two minutes' silence on 30 January, Martyrs' Day. A whole nation pausing together is close to what Neruda imagines.

topics.title: A strange, exotic moment of peace

learn.hook: No engines. No rush. Fishermen sparing whales. Generals changing into clean clothes. Neruda paints a world on pause.
points: It would be an exotic moment, without rush and without engines; we would all be together in a sudden strangeness.
Fishermen in the cold sea would not harm whales.
The man gathering salt would look at his hurt hands, noticing his own pain for once.
Those who prepare green wars, wars with gas and fire, victories with no survivors, would put on clean clothes and walk with their brothers in the shade, doing nothing.

example.q: What does the image of the salt gatherer show?
steps: He works so hard that he never notices his injuries.
In the quiet moment he looks at his hurt hands.
Stillness lets people notice their own suffering.
example.answer: That constant work makes us ignore our pain; silence lets us see and care for ourselves.

learn.reallife: Workers in the salt pans of the Rann of Kutch, the Agariyas, are known to suffer injuries to their hands and feet from salt. Neruda's salt gatherer is real.

topics.title: Not death but life: the earth's lesson

learn.hook: Does Neruda want us to stop living? No. He wants us to stop rushing, which is very different.
points: The poet says he does not want total inactivity; life is what it is all about, and he wants nothing to do with death.
If we were not so single-minded about keeping our lives moving, a huge silence might end the sadness of never understanding ourselves and of threatening ourselves with death.
The earth can teach us: when everything seems dead in winter, it later proves to be alive in spring.
Ending: the poet counts to twelve, asks us to keep quiet, and leaves.

example.q: What lesson does the earth teach us?
steps: In winter, trees and fields seem dead.
So stillness is not death; it can be a time of renewal.
example.answer: Apparent stillness can hold hidden life; like the earth, silence can renew us.

learn.reallife: A field after harvest in Punjab looks dead, but with the next sowing it is green again. Neruda's earth lesson is something every Indian farmer knows.

learn.hook: Neruda's poem is short, but it touches war, ecology and the human mind all at once.
points: Silence and introspection: a pause lets us look within and understand ourselves.
Universal brotherhood, peace and non-violence: no language barriers; warmongers walking with their brothers.
Criticism of war, harm to nature and mindless activity: green wars, harming whales, endless rush.
Form: free verse and direct address to the reader with 'let us' and 'we', which includes everyone.

example.q: How does the poet promote universal brotherhood?
steps: Everyone keeps still at once, all over the earth.
No one speaks any language, removing barriers.
Former enemies walk together as brothers.
example.answer: By imagining all humanity sharing one silent moment, without language barriers or war, as brothers.

learn.reallife: Yoga and meditation, traditions with roots in India, now practised worldwide, value the same pause and introspection that Neruda praises.

learn.hook: Repeated 'without', fishermen, whales, a salt gatherer: Neruda builds his message image by image.
points: Anaphora and repetition: lines starting the same way ('without rush, without engines') stress the absence of noise and haste.
Imagery: fishermen and whales, the salt gatherer, the warmongers; each shows a different harm we could pause.
Personification of the earth, which can 'teach' us; paradox of life hidden under apparent death.
Counting to twelve and keeping still would help us find peace, introspection and brotherhood. Twelve is often read as the hours on a clock face or the months of a year, a full cycle of time.
The poet does not advocate total inactivity or death: he says life is what it is all about.

example.q: Explain the paradox in the earth's lesson.
steps: A paradox seems self-contradictory but holds a truth.
Truth: rest and stillness hide life and renewal.
example.answer: It seems contradictory that dead things are alive, but in nature dormancy leads to new life; so silence can renew us.

learn.reallife: A neem tree sheds its leaves and stands bare, then bursts into fresh green leaves a few weeks later. That is the paradox of the earth that Neruda uses.

learn.hook: 'What sadness does the poet refer to?' is one of the most-asked short questions on this poem.
points: The sadness: never understanding ourselves and threatening ourselves with death, caused by constant, mindless activity.
Symbol from nature: the earth, which seems dead but later proves to be alive, showing life under apparent stillness.
Lines that best convey the message: the call to count to twelve and keep still, and the line on life being what it is all about.
Extract-based MCQs ask about devices and meanings; short answers should link silence with introspection and peace.

example.q: Extract (paraphrased): 'If we were not so single-minded about keeping busy, a huge silence might end our sadness.' Which sadness?
steps: Read the context: we never understand ourselves.
We also threaten ourselves with death through war and harm.
example.answer: The sadness of never understanding ourselves and of threatening ourselves with death.

learn.reallife: Exam halls in India go silent before the paper starts. Many toppers say that minute of calm helps them think clearly, a small-scale 'Keeping Quiet'.
